title: Insider-Trading Watchdog for Entertainment Announcements
one_liner: Sportradar-style integrity monitoring for game publishers, studios and awards bodies whose announcements and results now trade as prediction-market contracts.
customer: Legal and compliance teams at game publishers, film and TV studios, awards bodies, esports leagues and streamers. Prediction-market exchanges are a secondary buyer.
problem: Kalshi valuation went from about $11B to $22B between Dec 2025 and May 2026, and entertainment and awards are already about 11% of activity. Employees, agencies, vendors and journalists under embargo hold non-public information that now has a price. No one monitors it, and sports leagues already pay for integrity services that entertainment lacks.
solution: Map every listed contract on Kalshi, Polymarket and other venues to the client's titles, awards and announcements. Detect abnormal volume and price moves ahead of reveals, and deliver incident packets for counsel. Add embargo-tier employee policy and training, and give exchanges a restricted-list API.
why_now: Prediction markets are expanding beyond sports despite state fights, and regulators will demand integrity partners as entertainment contracts multiply.
revenue_model: $2-10k per month subscriptions for IP owners, exchange-side API fees, and forensic investigations at project rates.
non_obvious_insight: Publishers think prediction markets are a gambling issue for someone else. For the first time, their 5,000 employees and 300 vendors hold embargoed information worth money. Sports solved this with third-party integrity vendors, and entertainment has none.
first_30_days: Build a tracker of all entertainment and gaming contracts across major venues. Publish a report on volume spikes before announcements. Contact compliance heads at 10 publishers and awards bodies, and sell one 3-month pilot at $5k per month.

title: Delay Insurance for Data Center Energization
one_liner: Parametric insurance and pricing data that pay developers and lenders when the utility misses its committed energization date.
customer: Data center developers, construction lenders and hyperscale tenants with delivery-date penalties. Reinsurers supply the capital.
problem: A delayed 60 MW site costs about $14M a month. Utilities commit to dates that slip, standard delay-in-start-up cover excludes utility delay, and developers cannot hedge the largest schedule risk in the AI buildout.
solution: Build a database of utility energization performance (committed versus actual dates) by utility and substation type. Write parametric cover with the trigger set at the utility's committed date plus N days, under an MGA or coverholder structure with a Lloyd's or reinsurance backer. Also sell a 'time-to-power index' to lenders and developers.
why_now: The hyperscale pipeline is huge, waits reach years, and new large-load tariffs formalize committed dates, so the risk is finally observable in public filings.
revenue_model: Premium of roughly 2-5% of limit a year, with 15-20% MGA commission, plus data subscriptions from lenders and developers.
non_obvious_insight: Delay looks uninsurable only until you notice it is parametric. The trigger is the utility's own date, which the developer cannot move, and it is currently priced by gut.
first_30_days: Compile a dataset from ~200 public PUC and utility large-load filings. Publish a free 'Time-to-Power Index' teaser. Meet three MGAs or coverholders. Pitch 10 lenders. Land one design-partner letter of intent.

title: DNA-Certified Coral Frag Registry
one_liner: A genotype registry where reef breeders register mother colonies and buyers verify that a $500 frag is genuinely the named morph.
customer: Coral breeders and vendors, frag-swap organizers, high-end reef hobbyists and aquarium auction sites.
problem: Frags are clones, so one genotype circulates under multiple names and different colonies share a name. Studies of aquarium-trade corals show named morphs and common names are messy, and DNA barcodes do not resolve Acropora from the trade. High-value morphs sell for hundreds to thousands of dollars with no provenance.
solution: Genotype tissue clippings with low-cost SNP or amplicon panels through a partner lab. Breeders register mother genotypes with their signature, buyers mail a clipping (~$40) for a match, vendors display a 'DNA-verified' badge, and a searchable registry prevents duplicate naming and supports lineage and royalty claims.
why_now: Cheap sequencing and ML-based genotype calling make per-sample cost low enough for hobbyists. The research gap between barcodes and genotype identification is now documented.
revenue_model: $40 per verification, $99 breeder registration, a $29/month vendor badge subscription, and royalties on licensed morphs.
non_obvious_insight: In clonal organisms the genotype is the product, yet the market prices names, which are marketing. The first to make genotype searchable creates something like a plant-variety registry, which breeders will fund because it protects their premium. Expect challenges from species-specific panels, symbiont DNA and shipping rules.
first_30_days: Partner with a genomics lab. Test 100 frags from 5 well-known vendors' same-name corals for free and publish any duplicate genotypes sold under multiple names in reefing forums. Sell the first 300 paid tests.

title: Percentage-Rent Rails for Small Retail Strips
one_liner: Sales-linked leases with rent automatically swept from the tenant's POS, so independent landlords can fill dark restaurant and shop spaces and tenants stop dying under fixed rent.
customer: Owner-operator landlords of neighborhood retail strips and mixed-use buildings with vacancy, and independent restaurants and retailers seeking space. Platform revenue comes from landlords and processed rent.
problem: Higher rates and a squeezed consumer are closing independents. Landlords face 6-12 months of vacancy and costly tenant improvements. Percentage-rent leases align risk, but small landlords do not trust tenants' sales reports, so the structure has been confined to big malls.
solution: A standard 'base plus percent' lease template (a lower base of about 50-60% of market plus 5-8% of gross sales above a breakpoint). Rent is computed and swept automatically from Toast, Square or Clover data with tenant consent, and the landlord sees a live dashboard. Add leasing and brokerage, and a lender-facing cash-flow report so landlords can refinance on more predictable income.
why_now: Refinancing at higher rates pushes landlords to prefer occupied space. Rates just rose again and the consumer is K-shaped. POS APIs and embedded payments now make sales reporting verifiable and rent collection automatic for small operators.
revenue_model: 1-2% of rent flow processed, a leasing commission on placements, and a lender-reporting subscription. Optional financing spread for landlords.
non_obvious_insight: Percentage rent died in small retail because of an information problem, not an economics problem, and POS data solves the information problem. Because landlord income scales with tenant sales, the system flips the landlord from adversary to partner and wins in booms as well as downturns.
first_30_days: Recruit three landlords with vacant restaurant or retail spaces in one metro. Have a lawyer draft the lease template. Build Toast and Square OAuth plus ACH sweeps with existing tools. Sign two tenants on sales-linked leases and use their first rent runs as proof.

title: Recovery Units: Hospital Step-Down in Lease-Up Apartments
one_liner: Master-lease vacant units in lease-up apartment buildings near hospitals and rent them by the night as staffed 7-30 day recovery apartments for patients who have no safe home to be discharged to.
customer: Hospital care-management and ACO budgets, plus Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans, pay per diem. Apartment owners get guaranteed rent.
problem: Hospitals hold medically ready patients because home is unsafe, absent or far away. Those avoidable days are commonly cited at $2,500+ each, skilled-nursing beds are scarce, and hospital-at-home programs exclude patients without a suitable home. In the same metros 1.2M apartment units sit in lease-up, with concessions on about 16% of stabilized units (21% in the South, 37% in Austin). Owners of stalled lease-ups need occupancy and real rent, not another free month.
solution: A 10-20 unit block per hospital cluster: furnished, accessible, with home-health nursing and PT visits, meal delivery, a caregiver check-in line and a nurse-led transition plan. Bill a bundled per diem of roughly $175-300 against the $2,500+ hospital day. Owners get a 12-24 month master lease at near face rent with no concession.
why_now: The 2026 lease-up glut and 34-day lease times make owners receptive to any non-haggling tenant. Enhanced ACA subsidies expired and Medicaid work requirements arrive in Jan 2027, so hospitals face rising uncompensated care and margin pressure and are hunting for cheaper post-acute options.
revenue_model: Per-diem revenue minus master-lease and service costs (illustratively $50-80/day margin at 70% occupancy); later capitated arrangements with plans.
non_obvious_insight: A lease-up owner values a tenant that pays full rent on a unit that would otherwise carry a concession, and a hospital values the cheapest safe bed it has ever been offered. The two budgets have never touched because no one operates in between.
first_30_days: Find one lease-up property within 5 miles of a hospital that is running 20%+ concessions. Negotiate 5 units on a 6-month master lease with a 60-day out. Sign a home-health agency. Pitch the hospital's case-management director to trial 10 discharges and invoice per diem in month 2. Check local short-stay rules first and use a 30-day minimum license with early-release credits where needed.

title: Restock Monitors Turned Competitor Sell-Through Radar
one_liner: Repurpose the Discord restock-monitor infrastructure teen resellers run into a SKU- and size-level sell-through index for DTC brands and the investors and acquirers who buy them.
customer: Founders and merchandisers of DTC brands who want to see rivals' sell-through ($199 to $799 per month), boutique retail buyers, and consumer-focused funds, search-fund buyers and e-commerce acquirers who need diligence on a Shopify brand ($2,000 to $5,000 per report).
problem: Everyone in e-commerce has to guess how fast a competitor's hero product actually sells. Public analytics tools give traffic estimates, not sell-through by size, color or restock. Buyers of small Shopify brands take the seller's word for 'we sell out in days' and get burned.
solution: Teen resellers already run monitors on thousands of storefronts: each one polls public product feeds so a Discord ping fires the instant a size restocks. The same stream, kept as history, shows how fast each variant flips to sold-out, restock cadence, drop timing, markdown timing, price changes and collection moves. Package it as a weekly Sold-Out Index and an on-demand brand report: 'their black M hoodie sold out in 41 minutes twice, restocked every 3 weeks, and they cut price 15% after the tariff news'. Use public storefront signals only, with no checkout tricks, and honor rate limits and terms.
why_now: Tariff-driven price changes in 2025-26 have every brand asking what rivals did to prices and when. DTC brand acquisition and roll-up activity means more diligence is being done on tiny Shopify brands. LLMs now classify messy product titles into a clean taxonomy cheaply, which was the hard part of turning monitor pings into an index.
revenue_model: Subscription for brand and retail buyers ($199 to $799 per month), one-off diligence reports ($2,000 to $5,000), and a data feed for funds later.
non_obvious_insight: The restock-alert economy is really an accidental, huge, always-on sensor network for the long tail of DTC commerce. Enterprise alt-data vendors ignore small brands because they think there is no data on them. Resellers have been logging exactly that data every minute for years. The unit of value is sold-out speed by variant, which reseller monitors track and analytics vendors do not.
first_30_days: Take the existing monitor feed for about 2,000 storefronts in streetwear, sneakers and collectibles and start logging history now, because history is the asset. Publish a free weekly Sold-Out Index thread on TikTok and X to get inbound. Sell 10 founders a $199 competitor watchlist by DM. Pitch one search-fund or acquirer community for a paid diligence report at $2,000 to check willingness to pay.

title: Launch and Reentry Airspace Forecasts for Airlines
one_liner: A dispatcher-facing forecast of whether launch and debris closures will really happen, and what rerouting will cost.
customer: Airline operations control centers on Caribbean, Atlantic and Pacific routes, cargo airlines, business-jet operators and flight-planning software vendors.
problem: Launches hit 321 in 2025, and Starship debris in early 2025 disrupted flights around Florida and the Caribbean. Launch slips and scrubs make late notices unreliable. Dispatchers over-buffer fuel and time or get surprised, and there is no probabilistic view of hazard areas.
solution: An API and dashboard that fuses launch manifests, vehicle-specific slip and scrub statistics, trajectory and debris-response-area models, and reentry predictions. It outputs closure probability and expected reroute cost per flight. Deliver it into existing flight-planning tools as a plug-in.
why_now: Cadence is climbing (223 launches in 2023 to 321 in 2025), Starship is flying orbital profiles, and new vehicles such as New Glenn and Stoke's Nova are coming. Airspace impact scales with cadence.
revenue_model: $30-150k per year per airline. Per-flight API fees through flight-planning vendors. Cargo and charter tiers.
non_obvious_insight: The valuable prediction is not where the hazard area is but whether the launch will actually go, which is a schedule-slip model. That converts publicly available manifests into a decision-quality product.
first_30_days: Backtest a slip and scrub model on the last 12 months of Florida and Vandenberg launches. Show it to five dispatch managers at airlines flying Caribbean routes. Offer a free pilot on one route and a paid tier for the next quarter.

title: PFAS-Cleared Succession for Plating Shops
one_liner: Fixed-price wastewater and PFAS readiness reports that let retiring plating and anodizing owners sell to buyers and lenders, feeding a buyer marketplace.
customer: Retiring owners of metal-finishing shops, industrial business brokers, SBA lenders and search-fund or roll-up buyers, at $9-18k per report plus a success fee.
problem: About 60% of manufacturing firms have owners aged 55+, and reshoring and defense customers cannot find finishing capacity (plating, anodizing, passivation). Wet-process shops carry discharge permits, sludge records and historic PFAS exposure that stall buyers' and lenders' diligence, so shops close instead of transferring.
solution: A standardized wet-shop report covering permit and sewer-use history, a PFAS use inventory and sampling, sludge manifests and quoted closed-loop upgrades. Add a clean-up and certification package, then match certified shops to buyers.
why_now: Reshoring is happening inside existing buildings. POTWs are hunting PFAS sources ahead of 2027 monitoring. Compass-type roll-ups are buying shops, and the MMS admits no dataset of owners near retirement exists.
revenue_model: Report fee, 1% success fee on transactions, and remediation referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The real reshoring bottleneck is finishing, not machining. Finishing shops cannot change hands because water liabilities are unpriced, so whoever prices them owns the deal flow.
first_30_days: Call 10 industrial business brokers and the metal-finishing trade association. Do two discounted reports. Publish a one-page checklist to build a lead list of owners.

title: Training-Day School Inside Youth Sports Facilities
one_liner: Turn the empty weekday hours of club-sports facilities into ESA- and scholarship-funded microschools for serious young athletes.
customer: Owners of independent indoor youth-sports facilities (volleyball, gymnastics, basketball, hockey, tennis/pickleball, swim) in ESA and voucher states such as AZ, FL, TX and UT. Tuition is paid by families out of ESA, voucher or (from 2027) scholarship-granting-organization funds.
problem: Facilities carry rent and HVAC costs but sit idle roughly 8am-3pm on weekdays, because their revenue is concentrated in evenings and weekends. Families spending thousands a year on club sports fight school schedules, travel and early mornings. Microschool compliance (registration, occupancy, insurance, ESA vendor status) is daunting for a gym owner. School status also matters financially: in Texas, registered private-school kids get about $10,474 in ESA money while homeschoolers get about $2,000.
solution: A turnkey 'training-day school' kit. It includes state-specific school registration and a change-of-occupancy checklist, a low-screen paper-based mastery curriculum from a partner, hiring and training of a credentialed lead teacher plus coach-guides, insurance, ESA/SGO vendor enrollment and tuition billing. The daily schedule is 3 hours of academics plus 3 hours of training. Opt-in wearable sleep and load data decides when the hard academic blocks and the hard training blocks fall. The facility fills 20-40 seats at ESA-level tuition during dead hours.
why_now: ESA money is scaling (Texas had 200k+ applicants). The federal $1,700 scholarship tax credit starts in 2027 with 31 states opted in, yet about 1,000 microschools are in limbo awaiting Treasury rules, so operators want ready-made compliance. Alpha School (about 50 campuses, heart-rate monitors) has shown parents will pay for short academics plus afternoon workshops. 61% of teachers now want less device use, and homeschooling is transient (about 30% do it for 1-2 years), so hybrid products fit.
revenue_model: $12-20k setup fee per facility plus 8-10% of tuition, or $1.5k/month SaaS plus billing fees. A site with 25 students at $8-10k is about $200-250k of tuition a year, so roughly $20k a year recurring to us per site. Add referral fees on curriculum and insurance.
non_obvious_insight: Alpha School sells a schedule, not a building. The scarcest inputs (a big safe space, coaches, motivated kids, parents with athletic budgets) already exist in every metro at sports facilities that lose money on weekdays. Boarding sports academies cost $70k+; the mid-market, ESA-priced version does not exist yet, and the gating constraint is building code, so the wedge is a compliance kit for the friendliest states.
first_30_days: Pick one state with microschool-friendly occupancy rules (for example Arizona or Florida). Contact 40 facility owners through club-owner groups and facility trade associations and sign 2-3 letters of intent. Pre-enroll 10-15 athlete families with $500 deposits for a January semester. Hire a part-time certified teacher as head of school, and use an existing curriculum partner plus a lawyer-reviewed compliance template.

title: Code-Upgrade Packages for Home Daycares
one_liner: Fixed-price, state-specific remodel packages plus permit navigation that help licensed in-home daycares climb to the next capacity tier, for example 6 to 12 kids.
customer: Licensed family child care providers (capacity 4-8) who want to add slots. Projects are financed by CDFI or SBA microloans, state facility grants, or employers buying slots under the expanded 45F credit.
problem: Family homes are the fastest-growing licensed supply (+4.3% in 2024) versus +1.5% for centers, but growth stalls at capacity thresholds where code and licensing rules jump (egress, fire separation and alarms, second exit, restroom count, fenced yard). Providers face 3-6 agencies (zoning, building, fire, health, licensing) and small builders do not want $6K jobs. The supply map is measured in licensed slots, so this stall is invisible to policy.
solution: Ship a 'capacity ladder' of productized scopes per state (Step 1: 6 to 8 kids, Step 2: 8 to 12). Each has pre-drawn plans, a vetted small-contractor network on fixed prices, and a navigator who files zoning, building, fire and licensing applications. The provider repays from extra tuition, since two added kids at about $1,100/month each pays back a $20K job in roughly 9 months. A financing partner sits on top.
why_now: The 2026 45F credit (40%, or 50% for small businesses, with third-party and pooled arrangements; verify with tax counsel) gives employers a reason to fund slots. The dependent-care FSA rose to $7,500. Remodeling and HVAC slowdowns leave small shops idle and glad to take standardized sub-$10K work. Childcare costs $13,128 a year per child, so any added slot has an immediate paying buyer.
revenue_model: $299-499 code-gap assessment, 12-15% platform fee on each package (typically $6-20K total), permit-navigation fee, and financing referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Childcare supply is not blocked by demand or by providers' willingness. It is blocked by building-code step functions, which makes it a construction-scoping problem. Each extra licensed slot adds $12-15K a year of revenue at near-zero real-estate cost, far cheaper than the tens of thousands per slot for new center construction.
first_30_days: Pick one state and work through its child-care resource and referral agency to interview 30 providers. Sell 15-20 paid $299 code-gap assessments, catalog the three most common failures, and sign two small contractors to fixed prices. Close the first five packages, using assessment fees to fund the plan sets.

title: Backyard Telescopes as Cubesat Finders
one_liner: Pay owners of consumer smart telescopes to image newly deployed smallsats, so operators learn which object is theirs and whether their panels deployed.
customer: University teams, startups and small operators flying on rideshare missions with 100+ payloads, plus satellite insurers and brokers who want an independent health signal.
problem: After rideshare deployments the public catalog lags days to weeks and objects are mis-associated. A silent satellite may be dead or merely misidentified, and operators without their own ground networks burn weeks of contact attempts. 2025 saw 321 orbital launches and 4,517 satellites deployed, so far more unfunded small operators face this.
solution: A client for popular smart telescopes (Seestar and Unistellar class) receives tasking for predicted twilight passes and uploads wide-field frames. The server solves streak astrometry and photometry, returning position updates to improve the operator's orbit, an ID confirmation, and tumble rate and brightness changes that hint at panel or antenna deployment. Owners are paid credits per validated pass, with leaderboards.
why_now: Rideshare cadence and cheap launch flood the catalog with small, poorly funded payloads. Thousands of app-controlled smart telescopes now sit in backyards, AI streak detection is cheap, and the brief flags rising conjunction-screening load for operators.
revenue_model: $1,500-4,000 per mission for a LEOP identification and deployment package, plus a $500 per month monitoring subscription. About a third of revenue goes to observer payouts, and insurers pay per-object fees.
non_obvious_insight: The product is a fast, independent 'is it alive and deployed?' second opinion, not images. Space-situational-awareness firms build expensive sensor networks, whereas hobbyists supply sensors that are paid for in status and gear credits, at a fraction of the cost.
first_30_days: Use open-source astrometry and streak tools. Recruit 150 smart-telescope owners in maker forums and Discords. Take the public payload list of the next rideshare mission, cold-email 3 small operators with a free pilot, and convert two to paid at $1,500 on the following mission.

title: Screwworm-Era Rescue Transport Compliance Desk
one_liner: With screwworm confirmed in Texas, dogs leaving Texas and New Mexico need a fresh vet inspection certificate and destination permits; run the compliance desk that keeps shelter transports moving.
customer: Texas and New Mexico shelters, rescue transport organizations (ground and air), destination shelters in other states, and the funders who pay for transport.
problem: New World screwworm was first confirmed in Texas on 2026-06-03, with movement restrictions in infested zones across a growing list of counties. Reports say dogs from Texas and New Mexico now need a certificate of veterinary inspection within 72 hours of movement that attests no wounds infested with screwworm. Receiving states add entry permits and pre-travel inspections five to seven days out, shelter transports are slowing, and accredited vets are scarce for 20-100 animal loads.
solution: A transport desk with a destination-state rules engine, permit and eCVI orchestration, scheduling of mobile inspection crews (floating DVM plus techs) at pickup sites, a treatment log for authorized products, manifests, and rejection-risk alerts before a truck leaves.
why_now: Screwworm's first US detection (June 2026), FDA emergency authorizations for animal drugs (15 EUAs and 3 conditional approvals as of 2026-09-03), and state zone orders have changed movement rules mid-season. Shelters are crowded and funders are looking for what unblocks flow.
revenue_model: $15-35 per animal moved, mobile inspection crew fees, and SaaS for destination shelters. Costs often covered by transport grants.
non_obvious_insight: Rescue transport is treated as a charity logistics problem. The new binding constraints are regulatory paperwork and scarce accredited-vet hours, which is a compliance-ops business with per-animal pricing. The same rails will be reused for the next outbreak (H5N1, canine influenza, rabies rule changes).
first_30_days: Call 10 Texas shelters and transport groups. Put the top 5 destination-state rule sets into a spreadsheet. Run 2 transports with hired mobile-vet pickup inspections at $20 per animal. Approach transport-grant funders for direct payment.

title: Bone-First Strength Program for Women 45+
one_liner: A gym-delivered lifting and impact program for perimenopausal women, sold on DEXA-verified bone and muscle results.
customer: Women aged roughly 42-60 paying $79-149 per month, delivered through independent gyms, Pilates and strength studios and PT clinics that license the program.
problem: Women's fitness tech is fixated on cycle-syncing even though current evidence for cycle effects on performance is inconclusive, while midlife women (an 'invisible cohort' in sports science) face accelerating bone and muscle loss, worsened for those on GLP-1 drugs. Gyms sell toning and never measure the outcome that matters.
solution: A 24-week program of progressive heavy lifting, impact and balance work, with DEXA at baseline, 6 and 12 months via partner scan providers, simple bone-loading dose tracking with a hip or wrist sensor, coach training and a results dashboard studios use for retention. Positioned as wellness and performance with a physician advisor, not treatment.
why_now: Retail DEXA scans have dropped to roughly sub-$100, menopause is a mainstream topic, wearable makers are pouring money into women's health, perimenopause research is accelerating in 2026, and GLP-1 adoption has made bone and lean-mass loss a mass-market worry.
revenue_model: Member fees $79-149 per month; studio license $299-499 per month plus $30 per member; scan affiliate margin of $10-20 per scan.
non_obvious_insight: The moat is the outcome measurement: 'X percent of members held or gained bone density at 12 months' is a claim no gym can currently make, and the resulting dataset is valuable to clinicians and researchers. Cycle-syncing is a distraction from the larger midlife need.
first_30_days: Recruit 25 women aged 45-60 through two local strength gyms, book baseline DEXA scans with a retail or mobile provider, run a 12-week pilot with a physician advisor, and sign three studios to license the program off the interim results.

title: Vacant-House Concierge for Parents Moving Into Care
one_liner: One monthly plan that insures, inspects, maintains and eventually sells the house left empty when a parent moves to memory care or dies.
customer: Adult children and executors (45-65), often out of state, acting under POA or as executor. The channels are elder-law and estate attorneys, memory-care sales directors and senior move managers.
problem: When a parent moves into care, the house sits empty for 3-12 months. Homeowners policies typically restrict coverage after 30-60 days of vacancy, and pipes, taxes, utilities, break-ins and mail scams pile up. Probate cases rose about 32% from 2020 to 2024, and exhausted heirs are unprepared.
solution: A $199-449 monthly plan: vacancy-compliant insurance via an MGA partner, weekly inspections with water, temperature and entry sensors, autopay of utilities, taxes and HOA from an estate or POA account, seasonal maintenance, mail forwarding, sibling portal, documentation for the estate accounting, then cleanout, staging and a sell-when-ready referral.
why_now: The 80+ cohort is growing about 36.6% over the decade, senior housing is at 90% occupancy so moves happen in crises, and the $6T wealth transfer is underway. Heirs are far-flung Gen X executors who need a service, not a checklist.
revenue_model: Monthly subscription, insurance commissions, cleanout and staging fees, and a referral or flat fee on the eventual sale.
non_obvious_insight: Estate-settlement startups start at death, but the costly, uninsured window opens at the care move, years earlier. Anchoring on that moment gives access to the family before competitors and before the house loses value.
first_30_days: In one metro dense with senior housing, recruit 10 estate and elder-law attorneys and five move managers, secure a vacancy-insurance MGA quote, and sign the first 10 homes at an introductory rate.

title: Overnight First-Call Co-op for Independent Funeral Homes
one_liner: A shared night-and-weekend answering, dispatch and chain-of-custody service so small funeral homes never lose a call at 2 a.m.
customer: Independent funeral homes, especially 1-3 director shops. NFDA counts 15,401 US funeral homes, about 75% family or privately owned. Hospice and hospital partners are the second audience.
problem: Small homes burn out staff on overnight first calls or miss them. Each service is worth several thousand dollars: SCI reports average revenue per service of $5,985. Hospitals want fast pickups, and chain-of-custody mistakes are catastrophic in an industry facing scrutiny after high-profile scandals.
solution: A shared first-call desk with trained answering, dispatch to a vetted licensed removal network, and a QR-tag custody app (ID verification, photos, timestamps) from bedside to the home's cooler. Add a hospital-facing release portal and overflow transfers later.
why_now: Consolidators keep gaining scale while independents face labor constraints. Volume is flat (SCI -1.4% in Q2 2026), so each lost call matters. Post-scandal regulatory attention raises the value of documented custody.
revenue_model: Per-dispatch fees ($175-$400 by distance), $199-$499/month retainers, and software add-ons.
non_obvious_insight: Independents fear losing the call more than losing on price, and the call is decided in the first hour. Owning that hour makes you the switching layer between hospitals and independents.
first_30_days: Pick one metro. Recruit 10 independents and 3 removal contractors. Run the phone desk yourself and charge about $250 per call. Log every call to build a service-level report.

title: Status-Cliff Benefit Sold Through PEOs
one_liner: A confidential, employer-paid benefit that screens temporary-status workers for alternate immigration relief, tracks work-authorization cliffs, and pre-arranges counsel and family plans before a raid, TPS termination or EAD lapse hits.
customer: Payroll, PEO and staffing firms serving labor-intensive employers (home health, poultry and meat processing, hospitality, warehousing, construction, agriculture), plus the employers themselves. They pay $4-9 per employee per month or $60-120 per screened worker.
problem: Employers with workers on TPS, humanitarian parole, pending asylum EADs or DACA are losing headcount unpredictably. Terminations of TPS and parole programs hit hundreds of thousands of workers with little warning, and automatic EAD extensions ended for renewals filed after late October 2025, so employees now fall out of I-9 validity while renewals are pending. Worksite enforcement and I-9 Notices of Inspection (3 business days to respond) are rising. HR treats it as a compliance chore, then loses 10-30% of a shift overnight.
solution: A benefit package in four parts. (1) A dashboard that projects the work-authorization cliff by employee category and date, with I-9 reverification scripts that avoid discriminatory over-documentation. (2) Confidential relief screening done by a licensed partner attorney for each willing employee (family petitions, pending asylum, U/T visas, SIJS, cancellation, adjustment eligibility) with the employee, not the employer, as the client. (3) An emergency file for each participating worker: signed G-28 on file, memorized A-number card, standby guardianship documents for children, and a hotline for the first 72 hours after a detention. (4) An I-9 pre-audit and a 72-hour Notice of Inspection response playbook.
why_now: TPS and parole terminations, the end of EAD automatic extensions, expanded enforcement, and increased I-9 audits all converged in late 2025 through 2026. Employers can no longer treat immigration compliance as an annual checkbox, and existing I-9 software only tracks expiry dates. It offers no relief screening, no emergency response, and no employee-side counsel.
revenue_model: Per-employee-per-month benefit fee split between the platform and partner law firms (structured as payment to the firm for services rendered, with the third-party-payor consent required by the professional conduct rules), plus per-screening fees and a premium I-9 audit-defense add-on. PEOs and payroll firms get a distribution margin.
non_obvious_insight: The employer's real loss is churn, not fines. In screenings, a surprisingly large share of workers, often a quarter or more in my experience, have a path they never knew about, because no one ever asked in a confidential setting. A worker who is told they have a path stays loyal to the employer that offered it. The right buyer is the PEO's benefits desk, since PEOs already sell legal-plan and EAP riders through one procurement decision.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical (home health agencies, where TPS and parole terminations are hitting staffing hardest) and one state. Partner with 2 immigration firms that have screening capacity. Pitch 3 regional agencies and 1 PEO with a 60-day pilot: 100 employees screened for $6,000, delivered as a de-identified summary of how many have alternate paths. Use the pilot data (headcount saved, cases opened) as the sales deck for the PEO channel.

title: Conformity Cases for Learning-Enabled Robots
one_liner: A compliance workbench and pre-assessment service that builds the CE-marking safety case for machines whose behaviour comes from ML models (warehouse robots, cobots, humanoids) ahead of the new EU Machinery Regulation.
customer: CTOs and safety engineers at robotics startups and integrators (10-300 staff) selling autonomous mobile robots, cobot cells, agri-robots, humanoids and exoskeletons into the EU.
problem: The Machinery Regulation applies from 20 Jan 2027 and adds duties for machinery with self-evolving or learning behaviour and for cybersecurity (background, verify), with AI Act Annex I overlay dated 2 Aug 2028 in the tracker. Consultancies know ISO 12100 and 13849 but not how to argue the safety of a neural-network policy, notified bodies have no playbook, and startups cannot sell to EU customers without a CE dossier.
solution: Software plus an expert network: hazard-analysis templates for ML perception and control, runtime safety-monitor patterns (shielding, safe fallback, speed and separation monitoring), test evidence generated from simulation and field logs, and a traceable assurance case linking hazards to mitigations to evidence, mapped to Machinery, CRA and AI Act. A partner notified body does a pre-review.
why_now: Foundation-model-controlled and humanoid robots reached commercial pilots in 2025-26, and the regulatory dates arrive within months. Assurance-case methods from aviation and automated driving are mature but have not reached robotics.
revenue_model: EUR 25-80k per product safety-case project, $2-6k/month SaaS, and notified-body referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The blocker for deploying humanoids in Europe is not the model but an argument a regulator can accept. The first team whose safety cases are accepted creates precedent that competitors must copy, which is a durable moat.
first_30_days: Interview 20 robotics startups and publish an 'ML robot CE checklist'. Sign three design partners at EUR 10-15k for a gap analysis and recruit an ex-notified-body functional-safety engineer as co-founder or advisor.

title: Guardrail Gateway for Hotel AI Agents
one_liner: A proxy between hotel AI agents (voice, chat, booking) and PMS, POS and door-lock APIs that enforces per-action permissions, spend limits and human approval for irreversible actions.
customer: Hotel AI vendors that need enterprise trust, hotel groups' IT and security teams, and cyber insurers.
problem: Hotels are deploying agents fast (Dextr AI raised a USD 6.7M seed for hotel voice agents on 24 Sep 2026, and 109 AI use cases have been catalogued across 39 hotel systems). Practitioner commentary warns agents often hold API access built for trusted staff, so a prompt-injected guest message could trigger refunds, comps, rate changes or key issuance. PMS platforms have no concept of a scoped agent identity.
solution: An API and MCP gateway in front of PMS platforms (start with one that has a public API). It is read-only by default, applies caps on write actions (small refunds auto-approve, larger ones go to staff for approval in Slack or WhatsApp), redacts personal data, has a kill switch and keeps immutable logs. It ships with a red-team pack of injection attacks.
why_now: Agents are moving from pilots to production in 2026, PMS vendors are opening APIs, and agent protocols such as MCP are mainstream. Insurers and enterprise buyers are starting to ask for controls.
revenue_model: USD 49-149 per property per month, OEM licences to AI vendors, and insurer referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: In the agent gold rush the scarce item is the permission model, not the agent. AI vendors will pay for it as a sales enabler, and insurers will pay because it caps their loss.
first_30_days: Build against one PMS with a public API (Mews or Cloudbeds). Sign 2 hotel AI startups as design partners, and publish a red-team report showing injection weaknesses in demo agents (with permission) to earn press and inbound interest.

title: Landowner-Side Broker for Data-Center Land
one_liner: A conflict-free advocate that scores your parcel's power value and runs a competitive process, so the family farm isn't sold cheap to an anonymous LLC.
customer: Family landowners with 100-2,000 acres near high-voltage transmission lines or substations, in data-center-active counties, who are getting unsolicited offers. Each deal is worth $5-50M or more.
problem: Developers approach landowners through shell LLCs and landmen, with NDAs and options that lock the land up cheaply. Landowners can't tell whether $30K or $300K an acre is fair, because value now depends on grid interconnection position, water and fiber rather than acreage. Regional brokers don't know how to value power, so owners either sell too low or refuse offers that are actually good.
solution: A licensed landowner-side brokerage. A Parcel Power Score built from public transmission and substation data, utility large-load tariffs, zoning and moratorium status, water and fiber proximity, and an independent power engineer's review. It runs a competitive process to many site-selection teams and developers, negotiates terms (sale, option, lease, JV, decommissioning bonds), and represents only the seller.
why_now: Land purchases for future data centers reached about $6B in the first half of 2026, up roughly 79% from a year earlier (Avison Young), and sale offers in some places run up to 10 times agricultural value. Sept 2026 coverage shows farmers getting huge offers alongside a local backlash and moratoria that make timing and zoning risk decisive. The seller-side infrastructure has not caught up.
revenue_model: $5-15K representation retainer that is credited against a 1-2% success fee. On $10-50M deals this is $100-500K per closing. Optional fee for a second-opinion review of an existing offer.
non_obvious_insight: Land in this market is priced on power queue position, not soil. Buyers know it and sellers don't, and that information gap is the fee pool. Being seller-only and publishing the methodology makes you the trusted party for landowners and gives hyperscalers a pre-assembled, pre-screened pipeline they will actually prefer. The parcel data is a compounding asset.
first_30_days: Pick a cluster of counties around a substation or 345kV corridor in a data-center-active area (for example Ohio, Indiana, Georgia, Texas or Pennsylvania). Build parcel maps with public HIFLD and county data. Mail or door-knock 300 landowners with a free Parcel Power Score. Partner with a rural land attorney and an independent power engineer, get a broker license or partner with a licensed broker, and aim to sign 3 exclusive representation agreements. Send a one-page buyer package to 20 site-selection teams.

title: Off-Ramp Cohorts for AI-Companion Dependence
one_liner: Eight-week, in-person, non-shaming cohorts that help heavy AI-companion users rebuild human contact, sold to individuals and to employee assistance and counseling providers.
customer: Adults roughly 22-45 who spend two or more hours a day with AI companions (Replika, Character.AI, voice-mode chatbots), plus their worried partners and parents. Second wave: EAP vendors, university counseling centers and behavioral-health plans that have no protocol for this.
problem: Research suggests companions relieve loneliness in small doses but deepen it with heavy daily use; a two-year Aalto study of nearly 2,000 Replika users reportedly found heavy use raised the perceived cost of human relationships and tracked with more depression and loneliness. Lawsuits (Character.AI and Google settled the Garcia case in January 2026) and new laws (California SB 243 in effect since January 1, 2026, Washington HB 2225 signed in March) put the harm on the record, but clinicians have no playbook, users feel judged, and therapy waitlists are long.
solution: A harm-reduction curriculum, not abstinence. Week by week, participants audit what the companion provides (constant availability, validation, safe rehearsal), then re-home each need with a human equivalent: a weekly cohort dinner, a scheduled 'warm call' partner, rehearsal of hard conversations with a facilitator, and a graduated time-box on usage. Ten people per city per cohort, led by trained coaches with a licensed clinician supervising, screening for crisis, and referring out when needed. Pre/post measurement with a validated loneliness scale. Ends with a graduation dinner rather than a discharge.
why_now: Companion apps now have tens of millions of users, the APA flagged AI relationships as a major 2026 trend, and settlements and state laws have made 'what happens to heavy users' a public question. Operators under companion-chatbot laws need credible places to send users, and no incumbent exists. The EU AI Act provisions covering companion-style products are phasing in through 2026.
revenue_model: $395 per seat for an 8-week consumer cohort; $150-250 per seat through EAP and counseling partners; $1,200 curriculum license plus about $30 per participant for therapists and coaches who run their own cohorts; later, outcomes-based contracts with behavioral-health plans.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody pays to 'quit', but people pay to get more out of life, and the winning frame is nicotine-style harm reduction that meets the underlying need (low-stakes rehearsal, non-judgmental availability) with human structures. The competitor is not therapy, it is the AI, so the product has to be as easy to start as opening the app. Companion operators facing liability will eventually want a referral partner, which is a distribution channel nobody has built yet.
first_30_days: Recruit 12 participants from Replika, Character.AI and related communities with a screener asking who would try reducing use. Contract an LPC or clinical psychologist as supervising advisor and write a crisis-referral protocol. Run a 4-week pilot in one city in a cafe or coworking back room, charging $150. Collect pre/post loneliness scores and testimonials, then approach five EAP vendors and three university counseling centers with the data. Keep marketing to coaching and wellness, with no clinical claims.

title: Unfreeze Desk for Indian UPI Merchants
one_liner: A court-ready dossier generator and fixed-fee advocate network that unfreezes shopkeepers' bank accounts after a scam victim's UPI money passes through them, with a freeze-continuity layer later.
customer: Small merchants, traders, fuel-station owners and freelancers in India whose current or savings accounts get frozen because a scam victim's money passed through their UPI QR. They pay per case (₹3,000-8,000) or a ₹199/month subscription. Chartered accountants and trader associations are the referral channel.
problem: Automated cyber-fraud freezes catch innocent recipients. One Faridabad scam of ₹4.43 crore led to more than 36,000 frozen accounts, mostly small merchants. A Mumbai shop owner was frozen over ₹826 and spent over a month trying to get access back. A retailer's ₹8.26 lakh current account was blocked over a single ₹1,000 UPI payment. Relief takes months, and working capital, payroll and supplier payments stall.
solution: Merchants upload the bank statement and freeze notice, and software extracts the flagged credit, payer VPA, invoices and merchant-vintage evidence. It then produces a bundle for the bank nodal officer and police investigating officer, and a draft writ petition citing the Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Rajasthan High Court rulings that a merchant cannot verify each UPI payer. Partner advocates file and appear at a fixed fee, and the tool tracks the case. Phase 2: a 'clean receipts' setup (order-ID dynamic QR, invoice per payment, a separate working-capital account) and an NBFC-funded bridge advance against the frozen balance.
why_now: The Andhra Pradesh High Court ruled in July 2026 that authorities cannot freeze a merchant's whole account for receiving a UPI payment from an accused, and other High Courts have said the same. That gives a template-able legal remedy where before it was ad hoc. The Faridabad freezes and the Home Ministry review put the problem in the news. UPI acceptance among tiny merchants keeps growing.
revenue_model: Fixed case fee of ₹3,000-8,000 (unfreeze package plus advocate), a ₹199/month 'Merchant Shield' subscription that keeps an evidence dossier updated, and referral fees from NBFC partners for frozen-balance bridge loans. Later B2B licensing to UPI QR aggregators and bank merchant-onboarding teams.
non_obvious_insight: The merchant is not defrauded. The loss is working capital held hostage by a blunt automated tool that recovers almost nothing, so banks over-freeze. A Parliamentary Standing Committee found only ₹0.57 crore recovered out of ₹2,294.79 crore lost to cyber fraud in 2022, about 0.02%. So the freeze is structural false-positive management, not an anti-fraud problem, and the buyer is desperate on day one. Police in Faridabad said 'People come crying. Some had only ₹200 or ₹500 transferred to their accounts, yet the banks froze them.' Evidence: https://the420.in/faridabad-cyber-scam-upi-fraud-accounts-frozen-home-ministry/ and https://www.medianama.com/2026/07/223-merchants-bank-accounts-frozen-upi-payments-fraudsters-andhra-hc/.
first_30_days: Days 1-5: Build a WhatsApp intake bot and landing page in Hindi and English ('Account freeze ho gaya? 10 minute mein case file'). Sign 3 partner advocates in Delhi NCR, Mumbai and Hyderabad at a fixed split. Days 5-15: Template the dossier and petition from the three High Court rulings and have the advocates review it. Post explainer videos in Hindi and Gujarati on YouTube and Reels, and in trader WhatsApp and Telegram groups where frozen merchants already vent. Days 15-30: Close the first 20-30 paid cases, publish anonymized turnaround times, and approach two CA firms and one trader association for referrals. The design must keep filings with licensed advocates to avoid unauthorized-practice issues.

title: Night Ledger: Sleep Evidence for Live-In Aides
one_liner: A camera-free $35 bedroom-door sensor kit that logs every night-time awakening of a dementia patient, giving live-in agencies court-grade proof of sleep or interruption, and a case for the second aide.
customer: Licensed home care agencies with 20-300 24-hour live-in cases, starting with Medicaid-contracted agencies in NYC, Long Island, Westchester and northern NJ. Secondary: families who employ live-in aides directly. Agencies pay.
problem: Live-in aides are paid for 13 of 24 hours. That is legal in New York only if the aide gets 8 hours of sleep, 5 of them uninterrupted, plus 3 hours for meals. A dementia patient who sundowns, wanders and needs toileting at 2am makes that fiction. The only evidence of sleep is the aide's own signed timesheet. Agencies face wage class actions and NYSDOL claims. Aides are underpaid and quit. The night, the most expensive and dangerous stretch of care, is the least measured.
solution: Two or three battery-powered motion or mmWave sensors (bedroom door, hallway, bathroom, exit door) and a hub that phones home. There is no video and no audio, because aides hate being watched and families in some states cannot legally record them. Each morning it produces a one-page Night Report: the longest uninterrupted stretch, the number of get-ups, exit-seeking events, and a one-tap aide confirmation of what was actually done. Quiet nights support the 13-hour pay. Noisy nights trigger a pay correction and build a documented case for the plan to authorize split-shift (two-aide) coverage. Families get 2am exit-seeking alerts on the same hardware.
why_now: In January 2026 a New York court reopened hundreds of shelved 24-hour-aide wage claims against NYSDOL and granted class certification (Legal Aid and NCLEJ). Federal DOL has only proposed reinstating the companionship exemption (July 2025). The 2013 rule is still the law, private rights of action are untouched, and state law in NY, NJ and CA applies regardless. Sensors, BLE and mmWave chips are now cheap enough to rent per case. The oldest boomers turn 80 this year, so live-in dementia cases are growing.
revenue_model: $79 per active live-in case per month, with the sensor kit rented and shipped. A one-time $1,500 to $3,000 wage-liability audit for agencies is the entry product. Families add-on at $29 per month for night alerts. Later, a fee for documentation packages that support split-shift authorization requests.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone treats the 13-hour rule as a labor-cost fight. Insiders know the same nightly record is a liability shield for the agency, proof of a heavier case that can justify two aides billed at full rate, and evidence for the aide, all at once. Nobody has built it because the buyer, the agency, has spent years preferring not to have the data. A class action changes that preference. Cameras are the wrong tool. Aides quit over them, and door-and-hallway motion data is enough.
first_30_days: Buy 40 off-the-shelf Zigbee or BLE motion sensors and a Pi or cellular hub. Write a script that emails a Night Report. Sell the audit as a service to 3 small LHCSAs in Brooklyn, Queens or Bergen County through wage-and-hour defense attorneys and home care association meetings, by offering a free 2-week pilot on their five heaviest cases. Ask two worker centers to beta test with aides and give aides their own copy of the log. The first paid pilots should come from agencies that were just sued or received a DOL inquiry.

title: Reliance Ratings for SOC 2 Reports and Auditors
one_liner: A buyer-paid forensic desk that tells vendor-risk teams how far to trust a given SOC 2 or ISO report, and the audit firm that signed it.
customer: Third-party-risk and security teams at banks, health systems, insurers and mid-market SaaS companies that ingest hundreds of vendor reports a year. Cyber insurers and PE/VC diligence teams are the second wave.
problem: In March 2026 a whistleblower alleged that Delve, a YC-backed startup valued at about $300M, issued 494 near-identical SOC 2 reports with conclusions pre-filled and signed by two rubber-stamp firms. YC removed it in April, and Delve disputes the claims. Buyers now suspect every clean PDF. Manual checks of AICPA peer-review and NASBA licence records take about 30 minutes per report, so most teams skip them.
solution: The buyer uploads the vendor's report. We compare it with a growing corpus using fuzzy fingerprints of system descriptions, test procedures and exception language. We check CPA licence, AICPA peer-review status, firm ownership, address and staffing footprint, sample sizes, period length, carve-outs and subservice-organisation scope. Output is a reliance score, a one-page red-flag memo, and a continuously updated rating of audit firms based on exception rates, boilerplate share and peer-review opinions.
why_now: The Delve fallout in spring 2026 made every security team ask 'who signed this?'. Compliance-automation platforms now tie vendors to audit-firm networks at scale (Vanta reports about 16,000 customers). LLMs make reading and comparing thousands of 80-page reports cheap for the first time.
revenue_model: $200-400 per report on demand, $20-60k per year TPRM subscriptions, API licences to vendor-risk platforms, and insurer portfolio scans.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders treat the audit as a commodity input that automation has solved. Audit quality varies enormously and invisibly, and the vendor pays its own auditor. That is the same conflict that made bond-rating agencies necessary. The moat is the corpus of reports, which only buyers collectively hold.
first_30_days: Build the fingerprint tool on 200 public reports from trust centres. Publish an 'Auditor Firm Quality Index v0' from public peer-review data. Offer security leads free re-verification of their vendor stack in exchange for contributing reports to the corpus, starting with those exposed to Delve's customer list.

title: Flight Recorder for AI-Drafted Police Reports
one_liner: Vendor-agnostic middleware that captures the AI draft, every officer edit and timestamp, then issues a court-ready authorship record, the process-based 'human-made' proof creators lack, so prosecutors will accept AI-assisted reports.
customer: Police departments and sheriffs' offices ($60-150 per officer per year), city and county attorneys and DA offices that must vouch for reports, and public defender offices (per-case discovery audits).
problem: Tools such as Axon's Draft One write narratives from body-cam audio, and reporting in 2025 said original AI drafts are not retained (prior knowledge). California SB 524 (effective 2026) requires disclosure of AI use and retention of first drafts, Utah requires disclaimers, and King County prosecutors said in 2024 they would reject AI-assisted reports (prior knowledge). Defense has the same failure mode: a SOCOM analyst's chatbot fabricated a ship's cargo manifest that was formatted as an official intelligence summary, with no provenance layer in the workflow.
solution: A capture layer inside the report editor or records-management system logs the body-cam transcript hash, the AI draft, each officer edit as a diff, and time-on-task, with per-paragraph officer attestations ('I observed' or 'I reviewed'). It emits a signed content-credential-style record attached to the report, a redacted discovery packet for defense, and a DA-portal view that applies each office's acceptance rules.
why_now: State laws requiring disclosure and draft retention are in force in 2026. AI report-writing is spreading while DA acceptance remains the gate. Process-based provenance standards (C2PA) now exist, and GenAI.mil's 2M-user rollout shows the same official-looking-AI-text problem is arriving federally.
revenue_model: Per-officer SaaS, per-case discovery-packet fees to public defenders, and later federal licenses for labeling AI-assisted analytic products.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck to AI report-writing is admissibility and credibility, not accuracy, and the real gatekeepers are DAs, not police chiefs. A DA who publishes an acceptance standard requiring a verifiable authorship record forces every vendor to comply, so give the standard to DAs first and sell the ledger to departments second.
first_30_days: Get one DA's office in a state with an SB 524-style law to co-draft an acceptance standard. Prototype a Word and Google Docs add-in plus a records-system-neutral upload, pilot it with 2 small departments already testing AI report tools, and offer public defenders an 'AI-report discovery audit' service.

title: Dementia Desk: Ex-Aide Call Center for Banks
one_liner: A remote call-center pod staffed by former dementia aides, taking the confused, repeat and possibly scammed callers that credit unions and utilities cannot handle.
customer: Credit unions ($200M-$3B assets), regional banks, municipal and regional utilities, and pharmacy chains' member-service teams. The compliance or member-experience officer signs. Medicare Advantage plan call centers are the second wave.
problem: Front-line agents are scored on handle time. A caller with dementia asks the same question nine times, fails the security questions, insists a dead husband is in the room, or is being coached by a scammer sitting beside them. Agents correct them, hang up or escalate. That distresses the caller, costs the institution money and produces fraud losses. Free training exists (AARP BankSafe videos), but nobody takes the hard calls.
solution: A warm-transfer line. The agent presses a button on any call that sounds impaired and a Dementia Desk specialist takes over within seconds. Specialists are ex-aides with 5-15 years in dementia care. They use the aide toolkit: join the caller's reality, don't correct, redirect, never argue about facts, and verify later with the trusted contact. They can also tell when a second voice is coaching. Each call ends with a structured note: risk flag, trusted-contact action, card freeze, callback plan. The service also hands the institution documented staff training for the Senior Safe Act.
why_now: The oldest boomers turn 80 in 2026, so vulnerable callers are rising fast. AI voice-clone scams against elders spiked in 2025-26. The Senior Safe Act (12 USC 3423) grants a bank immunity for reporting suspected exploitation only if the staff were trained and the training is documented. Home care aides are leaving the field with back injuries and low pay, and remote work at $20-24 per hour is a real second career for them.
revenue_model: $9-14 per handled contact with a $2,000 monthly minimum. A $4 per employee per year Senior Safe Act training add-on. Later, a per-account fee for a 'trusted contact enrollment' outbound program that reduces fraud losses.
non_obvious_insight: The problem is not detection. Institutions already know who's confused. The problem is that nobody on the phone knows what to do next and every training video is passive. The scarce skill is de-escalating cognitively impaired adults, and the only people who have it at scale are underpaid home aides. This turns the labor supply that home care has been losing into a premium BPO product, and it gives aides a career path off their spines.
first_30_days: Recruit 8 ex-aides from CNA and HHA school alumni groups and caregiver Facebook groups. Write a 12-page call playbook from their own scripts. Offer two local credit unions a free 60-day pilot: agents warm-transfer any call they flag to a Google Voice line the pod answers, with a monthly report of fraud saves. Charge from month three. Ask the state credit union league to host a 30-minute 'confused caller' webinar as the lead source.
